title: A registry of DISPATCH ADAPTERS -- how one intelligence is started as a worker, and how what it produced comes back
description:
The hexagonal half of ADR-017 decision 2: the dispatch port knows no runtime, and a runtime is an ADAPTER. Like a runtime surface, this is the only kind of document allowed to carry a product's name, it is published in an adapter beside the kit, and the port finds it by the CONTRACT it keeps rather than by any list of publishers -- so a new intelligence is a new row in a new adapter and the port is never edited (Cardinal II, VIII).

A row is a DECLARATION and executes nothing (Cardinal IV). `starts.argv` is DATA -- a fixed argv with declared placeholders, no shell, no branch, no condition -- of exactly the class an activation block already names: the interpreter runs it and holds no knowledge of the product, the declaration holds no behaviour. The placeholders and return channels a row may name are the ones the PORT provides; a row naming any other is refused rather than substituted with an empty string, because a worker started with a silently blank instruction is the most expensive silence there is.

Everything a row says about somebody else's software is a CLAIM and stays one until a run of that product has been observed doing it -- which is what `says` is for, and why an adapter shipped before it has been measured is honest rather than green.

id.description: The id a packet's `route` names. One id, one declaration: a route that resolved to two adapters would be a name that is not a name.

says.description: Which product this starts, what is claimed about how it behaves, and where that claim comes from. Testimony, labelled as testimony -- including, explicitly, whether it has ever been observed on this machine.

starts.description: How the worker is started. The argv is run with its working directory set to the isolated workspace the port made for this task, never at the host root: the workspace IS the isolation (ADR-017 decision 5).

argv.description: A fixed argv. A part may carry placeholders in braces; the port substitutes only those it provides and refuses any other by name.

stdin.description: What is written to the worker's standard input, with the same placeholders. Absent means nothing is written and the stream is closed -- never an empty line that a prompt-reading process would take as an answer.

returns.description: The ARTIFACTS this worker produces, and the channel each is read from. Results come back as artifacts (A2A, adopted whole), never as a status message doing an answer's job.

from.description: The channel, by the name the port provides for it. An unprovided channel is refused, so widening the set is the port providing another one -- never an enum edited here.

completed_on.description: What this product's worker does when it finished the work, so the port need never DECIDE what an exit code meant. Anything else ends the task `failed`, with the code recorded beside the state.
